Mishnah (Shabbat 36b) opens: a kirah heated with straw/hay — one may place a dish; with olive-residue or wood one may not place until he rakes (garuf) or puts ash (ketum). The Gemara (38a) explains kirah is for two pots. The Gemara (36b) asks whether “one may not place” means “may not return,” but leaving is allowed even without garuf/ketum — Chanania’s view (that once it reached maachal ben derosa one may leave it even on an un-garuf kirah) — or perhaps the Mishnah is about leaving, so only with garuf/ketum is it allowed, and all the more so returning. The sugya debates at length without an explicit conclusion. Then (37a) R. Hoshaya teaches: if it was covered and then flared, one may leave fully heated water and a fully cooked dish — implying mitztamek vi’yafeh lo is permitted — but it is rejected because it was ketum. Similarly (37b) Rabbah bar bar Chanah in R. Yochanan’s name. Then (37b) Rav Sheshet in R. Yochanan’s name says: with residue/wood one may leave even not fully cooked; if removed, one may not return unless garuf/ketum — he holds the Mishnah is about returning, but leaving is permitted even without garuf/ketum. Rava supports: leaving is learned from “do not put bread in the oven near dark unless its face will crust,” implying once crusted it is permitted; returning is learned from Beis Hillel “even return,” and clearly they only permit returning with garuf/ketum. Rif concludes the practical conclusion is that “one may not place” means “may not leave,” so leaving also requires garuf/ketum; he brings proofs and rules against Rav Sheshet’s reading even though Rava supported it. Ran writes Razah refuted Rif’s proofs and Rosh agrees, though Rabbenu Yonah defended Rif; She’iltot and R. Yehudah bar Barzilai follow Rif. Therefore (per Rif/Rambam) it is forbidden to leave on an un-garuf/ketum kirah a dish not fully cooked, or a fully cooked dish that is mitztamek vi’yafeh lo; if garuf or ketum, one may leave anything (fully cooked or not), and certainly mitztamek vi’yafeh lo, since the decree is lest he stir coals and garuf/ketum removes that concern. Rashi relied on Rav Sheshet in R. Yochanan’s name and Rava’s support, and writes that our custom to leave on an un-garuf kirah is based on Chanania. Ran cites Rav Hai Gaon and Tosafos (in R. Chananel’s name) likewise; Maggid Mishneh (ch. 3) cites Rashba similarly; and Semag/Semak/Sefer HaTerumah/Hagahot (ch. 3) and Mordechai (Rosh haPerek) in Or Zarua’s name. Thus “cooked / not cooked is forbidden” (Shabbat 18a): for Rif it includes any dish that began cooking (even if it reached maachal ben derosa), and even fully cooked if mitztamek vi’yafeh lo; only fully cooked mitztamek vera lo is “cooked and permitted.” For Rashi, once it reached maachal ben derosa it is “cooked” and may be left; “cooked/not cooked” is only when it began cooking but did not reach maachal ben derosa. If entirely raw, all agree it may be left; and if one threw in a raw limb, it is like fully raw. This applies to pots; for roasting by a fire, raw meat is still forbidden (see siman 254 seif 4). Note: whatever is permitted to leave on an un-garuf kirah is also permitted on a kupach/tannur (Rambam ch. 3; Ran); those who distinguished “raw pot” between tannur and kirah rely on one Tosafos answer, but Tosafos elsewhere permit, and Semag/Semak permit both. Razah rules: the Mishnah is about returning; leaving without garuf/ketum is permitted only when the dish’s drying is not beneficial; for mitztamek vi’yafeh lo, if only maachal ben derosa it is forbidden; if fully cooked, there is a dispute and practice decides; and we follow Bnei Ma’arava who permit. Rosh writes: because opinions multiplied and Israel are attached to oneg Shabbat and will not accept stringency, leave them to the practice they adopted following poskim like Chanania.
The Tur wrote that “maachal ben derosa” is one-third cooking — so Rashi explains (Shabbat 20a and elsewhere). From Rambam (ch. 9) it appears it is half-cooked.

“Unless he raked or covered”: in the Mishnah — “until he rakes or puts ash.” The Tur’s “garuf” follows Rambam (ch. 3): removing the coals outward. Ran writes he agrees with Razah: sweeping coals to one side; if all coals were removed, even a tannur would be permitted since there is nothing to fear. Yerushalmi’s “sweep by hand” can mean only at the pot’s place. Ran also cites a Yerushalmi that “ketum” need not be complete: one need not cover until no fire is visible. Our Bavli also implies this: dimmed coals or a thin layer of flax tow counts as ketum; the baraisa’s wording “he put ash” (not “he buried in ash”) implies any covering suffices. Rambam (ch. 3) records dimmed coals/flax tow; I do not know why the Tur omitted it.

“If he put in a raw piece it is permitted”: Shabbat 18a — “if he threw in a raw bone it is permitted, for he removed his mind: he says ‘certainly it will not cook’ and he will not come to stir.” From the Gemara and poskim it appears this is only when one throws in a raw limb that cannot cook overnight — that is what makes him truly remove his mind. Rambam’s Perush haMishnayos writes one may put something raw such as meat or even vegetables; he implies that any clear act that signals “I’m not aiming to finish it now” serves as a reminder (like ketum, which can be minimal) so he won’t stir.
“But to lean a pot near it” — this is a Gemara question there, and it is resolved (permitted under the described conditions).

“If it was fueled with straw/hay, it is permitted to leave on it” — explicit in the Mishnah. Rambam (ch. 3) adds: if fueled with droppings of small animals, it is like straw/hay — implying large-animal dung is like wood. Yerushalmi in Perek Kirah states the opposite (small-animal dung like residue/wood; large-animal dung like straw/hay); perhaps their texts differed. Gemara (37b) teaches “two matching stoves”: if one is garuf/ketum and the other not, one may leave on the garuf/ketum even though it gains heat from the other.

“And a tannur — even if fueled with straw/hay — is forbidden” — Mishnah (Shabbat 38a) and a baraisa explain: in a tannur one may not even lean, certainly not on top, certainly not inside. Hagahos Mordechai: if the place is not yad soledes bo (not very hot), it seems permitted.

“Even if it is garuf u’ketum” — the Gemara implies garuf/ketum does not help for a tannur; Maggid Mishneh (ch. 3) cites Ramban and Rashba; Ran likewise; and this is the view of the poskim. Kolbo quotes Ba’al HaHashlamah that a garuf/ketum tannur is permitted; that likely refers to our side-opening ovens (treated like a kirah), not the Gemara’s tannur. Rambam (ch. 3) explains: because a tannur’s heat is very strong, one does not remove his mind and we fear stirring even a small remaining flame; one cannot rake out every spark; one may stir to extinguish remaining sparks. From this wording we learn that when it is mitztamek vera lo it is permitted even in a tannur (R. Yerucham vol. 3; Rif/Rosh imply likewise). I already wrote above that many poskim permit in a tannur anything that is permitted on an un-garuf kirah; even those who restricted “raw pot” to tannur admit mitztamek vera lo (since stirring cannot help). “Tannur” per Rashi: narrow above, wide below; the Bavli’s “more heat than a kirah” refers specifically to the top-opening tannur; Ran in R. Chananel’s name: our ovens are like a kirah (and “tannur of bakers” is mentioned in Bava Batra 20b). Kolbo: our “fornales” are heated inside, then fully raked, and since they are wide they have kirah status; similarly R. Chananel: our ovens are like a baker’s kirah.

“And a kupach (one-pot place)” — Mishnah: kupach fueled with straw/hay is like a kirah; fueled with residue/wood is like a tannur. Gemara: kupach retains more heat than kirah, less than tannur. This implies: with residue/wood it is fully like a tannur (forbidden even garuf/ketum); with straw/hay it is fully like a kirah (permitted without garuf/ketum) — so Ran and Rambam (ch. 3) write. One can ask why the Tur wrote that with straw/hay it is permitted only via garuf/ketum, since it should be permitted without — perhaps because Rosh rules the Mishnah’s kupach case is garuf/ketum (Rav Ada b. Ahava), and the Tur inferred the first clause is also only due to that; but it is not compelled. R. Yerucham (vol. 3) suggested that in our stoves there is no difference between one-pot and two-pot placements, so garuf/ketum suffices like kirah; I do not see why a “modern” kupach should differ from the Gemara’s (material changes do not matter). Ran notes that our hot-water ovens are like a kupach (one pot), and for a kupach garuf/ketum does not help (in the residue/wood case).

Rashi and R. Yona ruled that once it reached maachal ben derosa one may leave it on an un-garuf kirah; this is Chanania’s view. “One may not place” in the Mishnah means “may not return,” but leaving is allowed. They read the tannur/kupach mishnayot similarly: they are about returning, not leaving. I already explained when leaving is permitted according to them.

The Tur’s repeated phrase “for the night” can be read as not exclusive (also for tomorrow), since for tomorrow people usually insulate so it won’t cool, whereas for night they commonly do not insulate; or it can be read as literal (only “night”), and for tomorrow one may leave in more cases because he removes his mind from stirring. Kolbo and Hagahos Mordechai (ch. 2) are cited as allowing leaving for tomorrow even without garuf/ketum even before maachal ben derosa, since it’s “for tomorrow” — but I did not see other poskim make this distinction.

The Tur’s distinction between “leaving” and “insulation” is from Rosh in Perek Kirah. Ran cites the Geonim similarly, against Rashi’s comment on the Mishnah (“adds heat”) which Ran explains as if Rashi were reading the chapter as dealing with insulation. Ran rejects that: the sugya is about leaving (shehiyah), not insulation; therefore garuf/ketum functions as a hekker that he removed his mind from stirring. Maggid Mishneh (ch. 3) says Rambam holds the Mishnah is about leaving without insulation. Hagahot (ch. 3) also write: even if one may leave a pot on a kirah with burning coals, if he additionally insulated it in the usual way, he revealed he is particular it not cool, and it is forbidden — “we do not insulate in something that adds heat,” even if fully cooked — as Sefer HaTerumah and Sefer HaMitzvot write (against Ra’avya, who made no distinction). Mordechai (Perek Kirah) in Or Zarua’s name permitted leaving a pot directly on coals and even having a Jew remove it if he does not move coals; that assumes Rashi/Ra’avya’s approach. According to Rosh/Ran and those who distinguish, when the pot’s bottom touches coals it is considered insulation and is forbidden; the case where the pot is not touching coals but covered on top is discussed in siman 257.

“If one transgressed and left it…”: Gemara (37b–38a) asks: one forgot a pot on a kirah and it cooked on Shabbat — is it permitted? For Rashi/R. Yona this is when it cooked but did not reach maachal ben derosa; for Rif/Rambam it can apply even when it reached maachal ben derosa but is not finished; the adjacent question is when fully cooked but mitztamek vi’yafeh lo; if mitztamek vera lo it is permitted. Tosafos (one answer) says perhaps it is about totally raw and then concludes it would only be permitted in a tannur, not a kirah; Mordechai in the first perek records that. The Gemara concludes one may not eat it because the Sages penalized the forgetful (since people were leaving intentionally and claiming forgetfulness). Hagahos Ashiri: forbidden until Motza’ei Shabbat “enough time to be done” — Rambam (ch. 3) implies similarly. Then the Gemara asks: one transgressed and left — is there a penalty? Rosh writes the second question is like the first and is asked even after the decree — and asks whether they penalized only the person who left it or also his household; the Tur rules stringently and forbids everyone, even one who did not leave it. But in Mordechai’s Hilchot Shehiyah, it is forbidden only to the person who did it, not to others. Rif seems to read “transgressed and forgot,” and explains this second question as: if fully cooked but mitztamek vi’yafeh lo, perhaps they did not penalize the forgetful; it is not resolved and we are lenient — Rambam (ch. 3) likewise. The Tur objected to Rambam’s distinction (“why distinguish”), reading the Gemara as equating “intentional” and “forgetful” in the first question. That objection does not apply if the second question is specifically about fully cooked mitztamek vi’yafeh lo. I also wonder at Kolbo, who wrote that per Rif even if one intentionally left a fully cooked mitztamek vi’yafeh lo dish it is permitted — certainly if he forgot — since Rif only explicitly permitted the “forgot” case. Raavad reads “transgressed and left” as “unintentional (he thought permitted)” and it is even lighter than “forgot” (which is negligence), so even if fully cooked, “forgot” is forbidden.

Kirah garufa v’ketuma — returning: the Mishnah says Beis Shamai allow removing but not returning; Beis Hillel allow even returning. Rashi: returning is allowed since it is garuf. The Gemara (38a) says: according to the view that allows returning, it is allowed even on Shabbat.

“As long as it is boiling” — implies that if he held it until it cooled, returning is forbidden because it is like cooking; so the Tur wrote in siman 318. R. Yerucham (vol. 3, in R. Yonah’s name) adds: if most is liquid and it is cold when returned to the kirah and it further reduces, that is full cooking. Yet the Gemara implies that if it did not cool completely — even if it stopped boiling somewhat — returning is permitted. R. Yonah also says: returning is only when it reached maachal ben derosa erev Shabbat; if not, do not return it once removed. Maggid Mishneh (ch. 3) cites Ramban/Rashba similarly. Perhaps R. Yonah spoke of a case removed right at nightfall. The Tur in siman 318 holds: if not fully cooked, even if maachal ben derosa, further cooking applies even while still hot; therefore here returning is permitted only when fully cooked; if not fully cooked, returning is forbidden whenever the kirah’s heat still keeps it boiling.

“Only on its top” — Gemara (37a): “only on top; inside is forbidden.” Simple reading: if the pot’s base rests on the kirah’s walls and fills the cavity, that is “on top”; but if the pot is fully within the cavity and sits on the floor, that is “inside.” The Tur’s wording (“on its rim” / “on a cover over its cavity”) suggests he treats “on top” as on the rim or on a cover, and anything that fills the cavity counts as “inside.” Rambam did not state this explicitly; perhaps he relied on “we never return except on top of a garuf/covered kirah,” implying not inside.

“While still in his hand, and with intent to return” — Gemara (38a): “only while still in his hand; if he put it on the ground, forbidden.” R. Ami in R. Yochanan’s name permits even if on the ground; other Amoraim also dispute. Then Chizkiyah in Abaye’s name: first version — “still in hand” is permitted only if he intends to return; thus on the ground is forbidden even if he intends to return. Second version — “on the ground” is forbidden only if he does not intend to return; if he intends, it is permitted; thus while still in hand, even without intent, it is permitted. Rif ruled like the first version, and Ran explains: although the second is lenient, the Geonim ruled stringently because these matters are close to Torah violation; Rosh and R. Yerucham rule similarly; Maggid Mishneh cites the Geonim likewise — against Hagahot (in Sefer HaTerumah’s name) that one should follow the lenient view in rabbinic doubt.

Even if he did not place it on the ground but hung it on a stick, put it on a bed, or poured from urn to urn — the Gemara asked and left unresolved; Rif ruled stringently (same Ran rationale). R. Yerucham also rules stringently. Rambam (ch. 3) mentions only “on the ground,” not these questions — perhaps because it’s rabbinic and unresolved, so he was lenient there; yet he still forbids “on the ground,” since most Amoraim forbid. It is difficult that he did not distinguish intent vs no intent; perhaps he disregarded Abaye’s later distinction. Ran cites a Yerushalmi that these disputes apply only if removed erev Shabbat and not returned until dark; but if removed after dark, even if placed on the ground it is permitted to return. That clearly is not the view of Tosafos/Rosh (who forbid returning even erev Shabbat near dark) and Rambam writes explicitly the opposite: even when one may leave it, once removed on Shabbat it is forbidden to return unless it was not placed on the ground.

If it is not garuf/ketum, returning is forbidden: in the Mishnah, “do not place” clearly means “do not return” (the Gemara’s question was only whether it also includes leaving). Ran writes: even mitztamek vera lo may not be returned on a non-garuf kirah. Rambam (ch. 3) likewise: anything one may leave, if removed on Shabbat it may not be returned except to a garuf/covered kirah, or to a kirah/kupach fueled with straw/hay.

Not only on Shabbat: Tosafos and Rosh infer from “even on Shabbat” that Beis Shamai/Beis Hillel also dispute returning erev Shabbat in a garuf case; but in a non-garuf case, even Beis Hillel forbid returning even erev Shabbat. They then define a practical “measure” for erev Shabbat: when it cooled and there isn’t time to reboil before Shabbat. Ran rejects this and holds that on a non-garuf kirah it is permitted erev Shabbat for all, and that Rav Sheshet’s “even on Shabbat” means: even daytime Shabbat (not only night) — as Rashi explains. Rambam (ch. 3) also implies the prohibition is specifically on Shabbat (not erev Shabbat), which matches common practice not to be careful about erev-Shabbat return; R. Yerucham’s claim that Rif forbids near nightfall is surprising, as Rif’s words do not indicate that.

Rosh’s limitation: the erev-Shabbat returning prohibition applies only once the pot is fully cooked and placed merely to preserve heat until evening; then, returning it resembles the Shabbat case and is one decree. But while it is still cooking, one commonly removes/returns it during the day, so we do not decree. Tosafos (BMah Tomnin) write: we only forbid returning erev Shabbat when one removed it from a kirah he plans to leave it on and returns it there to continue leaving; otherwise one might learn to return on Shabbat; but if he returned it for insulation purposes, it is permitted (insulation rules are in siman 257). Hagahos Mordechai asks if one may place a pot initially on a garuf/ketum kirah near nightfall (perhaps erev Shabbat only returning is permitted, not initial placing). Hagahos Mordechai also writes: whatever is forbidden to leave near nightfall is likewise forbidden near “Barchu” (our Kabbalat Shabbat), but many great authorities disagree, therefore people were not careful. Tosafos also note the “leaning” sugya isn’t a proof for leaning against a fire, since kirah walls separate; yet Hagahos Mordechai and Hagahos Maimoniyos (ch. 3) permit leaning near a fire even near nightfall when a cold pot would not have time to reboil; this is only relevant where yad soledes bo — otherwise even on Shabbat it is permitted. Rambam (ch. 3) permits returning from kirah to kirah (even from low-heat to high-heat), but not from kirah to insulation nor vice-versa; Maggid Mishneh says this is from Yerushalmi. R. Yerucham reports a Yerushalmi that forbids moving between kirahs (as “initial placement”), while Tosafos say that erev Shabbat one may return in any manner since it’s garuf/ketum.

Tannur: the Mishnah implies returning into a tannur is forbidden even if garuf/ketum; likewise kupach fueled with residue/wood is like tannur. Rambam (ch. 3) rules: we do not return to a tannur nor to such a kupach even if raked/covered because their heat is excessive; Maggid Mishneh explains this even for mitztamek vera lo or when a raw limb was inserted — which may be left — yet returning is forbidden. Ran explains: returning always requires garuf/ketum, and for tannur/kupach that does not help. Our ovens may be treated as kirah. Rambam also wrote: wherever one may not return, one may not even lean — Maggid Mishneh notes some disagree and allow leaning on a garuf/ketum kupach (only tannur is stricter) — depending on the baraisa in Perek Kirah (“kupach with straw/hay: one may lean but not place on top; with residue/wood: one may not even lean”). Tosafos note that if the text says “one may lean,” it could be in a garuf case and “residue/wood” is a novelty; in any case, for Rambam, leaning is only forbidden where yad soledes bo. Hagahos Ashiri questions whether returning in error is like “forgot and left” (since the food was already edible); Hagahos Mordechai says any rabbinic violation of leaving/returning/insulating forbids eating unless the Gemara explicitly permits. Ran argues: even if R. Yehudah permits mitztamek vera lo in “leaving,” perhaps returning is different since it is an act on Shabbat; but Nimukei Yosef (R. Yona) says even returning mitztamek vera lo is forbidden (common pitfall: people “insulate” a kettle of hot water to pour into the pot, and sometimes one vessel is yad soledes and the other not, causing cooking). R. Yona (vol. 3) and Ran debate pouring boiling water into a pot; Mahar”i Abuhav explains that “anything that came into hot water” is for dry foods, but liquids that stopped boiling can have cooking again. Many forbid; one should protest. Hagahos Mordechai permits using an empty pot to “cap” the kirah and then set the hot pot atop it (and warns not to use a new empty pot due to whitening, and not to place the pot on the ground). Ran in Rashba’s name permits warming a fully cooked item like pandish atop a pot of hot water even if yad soledes (not normal cooking), but forbids insulating under clothes. Ran suggests that items not normally baked on a kirah may be warmed when mitztamek vera lo since it shows mere warming. Anything forbidden for a Jew is also forbidden via a gentile (amira is a shevut). Issues of fat, roasting-after-roasting, and all bishul details are treated in siman 318. Terumas HaDeshen 66 permits a gentile to place the hot pot inside a winter-oven and then light the fire to heat the room (even if cooled), but forbids a Jew doing the placement; Rashba (responsa) forbids telling a gentile to light a fire to warm one’s food as a penalty; practices about chuppah-ovens and gentile reheating are discussed. Finally, Shibolei HaLeket quotes (in Rashi’s name) our practice to rely on Chanania, and even cites R. Yeshaya’s further claim about insulating for tomorrow; but the later comment notes that many מפרשים disagree and the issue is treated in the next siman.
